15.0.1.en: God commanded His people to waive the debts owed to them by their brethren every seventh year (Lev 25:

15.1.0.en: It is called the Lord's release: in the seventh year God commands a release from all debts. He explains the meaning of the release, which is waiving all debts owed by companions and brethren, that is, by all of God's people.

15.2.0.en: The Law allowed them to demand that non-Jews pay their debts, so the rule of release in the seventh year does not apply to them, out of the Lord's care that the Jews should not be exploited by the cunning of the other peoples, who might borrow from them in bad faith with the aim of not repaying the debt, so that the wealth of the nation would gradually be lost; whereas the debts of the Jews to one another fall within the bounds of the nation itself, and if they are cancelled nothing of it is lost to the outside.

15.3.0.en: The preceding verses speak about the poor borrowing from their rich brethren. But if there is no poor person among God's people because of God's blessing on all in the land of Canaan, there will be no debts. But if someone borrowed for a sudden financial crisis and then returned and became rich, or borrowed to invest, he must repay the debts in the seventh year.

15.4.0.en: The blessings are conditional on the people's obedience to God's commandments, by listening to them and doing them, so that they do not withhold help from the needy among their people. Then they will be able to lend to the other nations while they themselves do not need to borrow from them; rather, they can rule over the other peoples through the success and progress they achieve, while no one rules over them.

15.4.1.en: Be compassionate toward the needy and the families who hide their need, and help them by not demanding debts, and do not forget that you are in debt to God for all the good things you own, and when you give, God gives you more, and when you forgive, God also forgives you.

15.5.0.en: Within any of thy gates: in one of your cities.

15.5.1.en: Nor shut thine hand: do not be stingy.

15.5.2.en: Thou shalt open thine hand wide unto him: help him and lend to him.

15.5.3.en: God calls them to help the poor, whether by almsgiving or by lending, that is, to be merciful to the needy.

15.6.0.en: A thought in thy wicked heart: you think a wicked thought.

15.6.1.en: Thine eye be evil against thy brother: you harden your heart against him.

15.6.2.en: And he cry unto the LORD against thee: and he complains of you to God.

15.6.3.en: God warns them against wickedness and the love of money, lest they refrain from lending to the poor man when the seventh year draws near, because he will probably not be able to repay and their money will be lost to them; for if they do this, the poor man cries out to God because of their harshness, and they will be wrong in the sight of God, and He will be angry with them.

15.7.0.en: Thine heart shall not be grieved when thou givest unto him: do not be unwilling when giving.

15.7.1.en: God requires His people to lend to the poor with willing, loving hearts, and God will bless them. This confirms the importance of giving with joy.

15.8.0.en: There must be poor people among the people, and God permits this so that the love of the rich for them may show itself in helping them.

15.8.1.en: The Lord loves the cheerful giver, so the more we rejoice in doing good, the more God rejoices in us, remembering that we give to Christ in the form of the poor and that together with the poor we are members of one body, and this makes our joy in giving firm.

15.9.0.en: If one of God's people becomes poor and sells himself as a slave, he works six years only, and in the seventh year he goes out free (Ex 21).

15.10.0.en: Thy floor: the threshing floor on which the grain crops are stored.

15.10.1.en: God commands that the slave be helped from the possessions of the rich man for whom he worked when he is released in the seventh year, so he gives him of his flock, and of the grain in his storehouses, and of the juice of his winepress, such as the wine and the oil, so that this helps him to begin a new life.

15.11.0.en: The Lord reminds them that they, the masters themselves, or their fathers, were slaves in Egypt, so their releasing their slaves is an expression of their thanks to the Lord who freed them from the slavery of Egypt. By remembering this great deed that the Lord did for them, they will have compassion on their brethren. And His saying "You were bondmen in Egypt" does not mean a particular generation, that is, only the generation that came out of Egypt, but applies to all the generations of the children of Israel in every age, for what happened to their fathers is as though it happened to them, or, had the Lord not freed the fathers, the sons would have remained under slavery.

15.12.0.en: The slave may prefer not to leave his master when the time of his release comes, because he has become accustomed to him and loves him and his household and has found rest in the good treatment he received during the period of his service to his master, so he prefers to continue and remain in service. Then his master performs a certain procedure, which is boring the slave's ear (considering that the ear points to hearing and obedience), at the gate of the city, so that it is a declaration before all the people, and the slave may not complain afterward that he is forced into slavery with this master. The same procedure is carried out for the woman slave (the maidservant).

15.13.0.en: Let this matter, that is, releasing the slave free in the seventh year, not be hard on you, because the value of his service to you during the six years equals twice the wage the hired servant would have received for his work with you during this period, because the hired servant spends only the daytime working, whereas the slave works all day, day and night. If you do so and release him free, the Lord will bless you in all that you do as a reward for your obeying the commandment. For God regards the Hebrew slave as a hired servant to his brother for six years, not like slavery among the Gentiles.

15.13.1.en: May you treat those who serve you in your house gently, as your brethren, and likewise those under you at work, and not be harsh to them, remembering God's mercies toward you.

15.14.0.en: The commandment obliged the believer to sanctify to the Lord the firstling of the offspring of his animals if it was a male (of the cattle and the sheep). And since it has become the Lord's property, it is not permissible to use it in the work of the field, nor is it permissible to benefit from the wool of those animals, for the same reason. So it is offered to God, remembering that God redeemed their firstborn in Egypt, so that they were not killed with the firstborn of the Egyptians (Num 3:13).

15.15.0.en: The firstborn males are slaughtered in the house of the Lord every year and eaten by the priests, while the firstborn females or the firstborn that have a blemish are slaughtered and eaten by their owners.

15.16.0.en: Firstborn that have congenital blemishes, whether this is lameness or blindness or any other bad blemish, are not offered to the Lord (Mal 1:8). For it is fitting that the best things be offered to the King of kings, not the meanest.

15.16.1.en: And this is an indication that the animal sacrifice is nothing but a symbol of the Lamb without blemish and without defilement whose blood would be shed on the Cross.

15.17.0.en: The hart: a kind of buck.

15.17.1.en: But these firstborn that have blemishes may be eaten in the place where their owners live, that is, in their homes, just as they eat the other animals not set apart for offerings, such as gazelles and harts, and it is not necessary in this case to follow the rules of ritual purity as is the case in religious feasts.

15.18.0.en: Once again he stresses the prohibition of eating blood, whether the blood of sacrifices offered as offerings or of those eaten as ordinary food, but the blood is poured out on the ground.

15.18.1.en: Be careful to offer to God the firstfruits of your time, your money and all your abilities and talents, and you will receive from Him blessings on all that you do and live in joy.

16.0.0.en: Passover: that is, passing over, and it is a memorial of the passing over of the destroying angel over the houses of God's people and his not killing their firstborn.

16.0.1.en: God reminds them to keep the Feast of the Passover in the month of Abib as a memorial of the redemption of their firstborn and their liberation from the slavery of Egypt, which symbolizes our liberation from sin by the redemption of Christ (Ex 12, 13).

16.1.0.en: The ritual of this feast includes the slaughter of sheep and cattle in the house of the Lord. The Book of Numbers

16.2.0.en: The Lord commanded that no leavened bread be eaten with the Passover meal for seven days, so nothing is eaten but unleavened bread, that is, bread without leaven, as a memorial of their going out of Egypt in haste, when they had no time to leaven the dough, and it was called the bread of affliction, that is, the bread of toil, as a memorial of the hardships, difficulties and opposition from Pharaoh that they faced in going out of Egypt. This is so that the events of that day, the day of their going out of Egypt, may be before their eyes all the days of their life.

16.2.1.en: Our Church, however, offers leavened bread in the sacrament of Communion, because Christ bore our sins on the Cross, and leaven symbolizes the evil which He bore for us and redeemed us.

16.3.0.en: God commands them that there be no leavened bread with them within the borders of their lands throughout the seven days, so the Jews on the fourteenth day of the month of Abib (Nisan) at noon would remove all leaven from the houses (Ex 12:15-17), before the slaughter of the lamb between the two evenings, that is, between the afternoon and sunset (Lev 23:5). And they had to eat the whole Passover lamb on the same night, that is, the evening of the fourteenth day, which is Thursday evening, and not leave any of it until the morning of the next day. And if anything of it remained, they had to burn it with fire.

16.3.1.en: This is what our Church is careful about in the sacrament of the Eucharist, as nothing remains of the Body and Blood of the Lord after Communion.

16.4.0.en: It is not right to slaughter the Passover in any place, but it is to be in the house of the Lord, that is, in the tabernacle of meeting or Solomon's temple. The lamb is slaughtered near sunset (that is, between three in the afternoon, which is the ninth hour by Hebrew reckoning, and five in the evening, which is the eleventh hour by Hebrew reckoning, that is, around sunset.

16.4.1.en: And between the slaughtering and the cooking and then the eating, a period of time will have passed that brings us into the evening of the day, which is the time of the going out of Egypt). The Passover is eaten between the two evenings, that is, between sunset and dark, at the beginning of the fifteenth day of the month of Abib (Nisan) (Lev 23:5).

16.5.0.en: Cooking the sacrifice for eating, that is, roasting it, must be done in the house of the Lord as was mentioned before, and then everyone returns in the morning of the next day, that is, after keeping the feast of the seven days of unleavened bread, that is, they return on the twenty-second day of the month of Abib.

16.6.0.en: The Feast of Unleavened Bread is connected with the Feast of the Passover, as the Passover is eaten on the fourteenth day of Nisan in the evening, that is, the night of the fifteenth of Nisan. And since the day according to the Jewish ritual begins from the evening of the previous day after its sunset until the sunset of the following day, the eating of the Passover takes place on the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, and the Feast of Unleavened Bread continues six more days after that, so the total days of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, including the first day shared with the evening of the Passover, is seven days, from the fifteenth day until the twenty-first day.

16.6.1.en: On the last day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, that is, on the seventh day, there is a retreat, so the believer does no worldly work, and separates himself from the cares of the world and devotes the day to holding religious rites and to worship.

16.6.2.en: Take care to partake of the Body and Blood of the Lord every week, and if you have the opportunity every day do not neglect it, so that you may be nourished and filled with the greatest power in the world and enjoy divine union and rejoice in His work in you.

16.7.0.en: To put the sickle to the corn: the beginning of the harvest.

16.7.1.en: The Feast of Weeks, also called the Feast of Pentecost, falls fifty days after the beginning of the harvest, which is on the second day of the Feast of the Passover. The Feast of the Harvest is called the Feast of the Firstfruits, in which the firstfruits of the barley crop, that is, the first sheaf of barley, is offered to God (Lev 23). The Feast of the Firstfruits symbolizes the Resurrection of Christ. The Feast of Pentecost, or Weeks, is held in thanksgiving to God for the crops they harvested, and symbolizes the feast of the descent of the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost, when there was a harvest and the joining of many souls to the faith.

16.8.0.en: The Lord commanded the keeping of the Feast of Weeks, rejoicing in the Lord and for the Lord. It is an agricultural feast in which the individuals of the people offer voluntary offerings according to their ability and what their means allow and the size of their crop, as the Lord gave them blessings and good things in the fruits of the land, from the crop of barley and wheat. The harvest of barley begins right after the Passover, followed by the harvest of wheat, and then comes the Feast of Pentecost.

16.9.0.en: Love feasts are held in which everyone rejoices in the blessing God has bestowed on them in the harvest of the land. The one who gives the feast includes in it the members of his household, that is, his son and daughter, his manservant and maidservant, and the Levite who lives in his city, and the stranger, the fatherless and the widow who live near him, and this takes place in the place of the house of the Lord. And in honoring the servants they remember that they were slaves in Egypt, so they have compassion on slaves and strangers.

16.9.1.en: The Christian is always joyful in the Lord's giving to him, and happy in God's grace here and then in his eternal inheritance in the Kingdom of Heaven, so thank God for all His gifts so that you feel their value and your enjoyment of them increases.

16.10.0.en: The Lord commanded His people to keep the Feast of Tabernacles for seven days, ending on the eighth day with a holy convocation. This feast is the third of the great annual feasts at which every male in Israel had to appear before the Lord in the temple. During it tents were set up on the roofs of houses or in the open country as a memorial of the dwelling of the house of Israel in the wilderness and their sojourning in it, where they lived in tents and were constantly traveling. One of the features of this feast also, as in the Feast of Pentecost, was holding shared feasts in the house of the Lord. This feast was held in the seventh month (Tishri) on the fifteenth day, four days after the Day of Atonement. They also called it the Feast of Ingathering because it fell at the end of the agricultural season when they gathered the rest of the produce of the land and the fruit of the slow-bearing trees.

16.10.1.en: There is a connection between the three great feasts, as follows:

16.10.2.en: The Feast of the Passover: with the first stroke of the sickle in the harvest.

16.10.3.en: The Feast of Pentecost: when the harvest is completed.

16.10.4.en: The Feast of Tabernacles: at the end of the agricultural year and the gathering of the fruits that ripen in the late summer season.

16.10.5.en: And this feast symbolizes for us, the believers of the New Testament, our sojourning in this world and our longing to set out toward our true, lasting homeland, which is heaven.

16.11.0.en: Here too is another new call to rejoice, for the Lord's will for them is that they rejoice and make the hearts of others rejoice with them. They are to rejoice in the gifts and blessings represented by the abundance of the crop and the multitude of fruits, and also to rejoice in giving to others, whether the consecrated, that is, the Levites, or the needy among the poor and strangers.

16.12.0.en: The Lord set the duration of the celebration at seven days. And "seven" is a number that points to completeness, and here it means complete joy. The celebration of the feast takes place in the place where the house of the Lord is, so the believer rejoices over the Lord's gifts and the blessings He has bestowed on him, and also rejoices that he gives to others of what he has.

16.12.1.en: In proportion to your love for God you are able to be a stranger to the material things of the world and to be content with little of them to meet your basic needs, and so you experience the work of God in you and rejoice, indeed you are able to make those around you happy.

16.13.0.en: God commands the attendance of all the males of His people at the three feasts mentioned above. What is meant by the Feast of Unleavened Bread is the two feasts of the Passover and Unleavened Bread, for their time is the same. The male represents the whole family, for he is a delegate for the females. The attendance of the males has spiritual purposes, which are:

16.13.1.en: 1- Strengthening their faith in the one God and in worshiping Him in His holy temple.

16.13.2.en: 2- Strengthening unity among all the tribes.

16.13.3.en: 3- Encouraging them spiritually by offering one worship together.

16.13.4.en: 4- Giving gifts to the needy, so that they do not come to these feasts without offerings to God of which the needy eat.

16.14.0.en: Each one gives of the offerings and gifts as much as his ability allows and according to his standing and in proportion to the Lord's blessing with which He has blessed him.

16.14.1.en: Remember that you will stand before God on the day of judgment, so do not stand before Him empty, but let there be acts of worship and works of goodness for you to present before Him, with all that you have endured for His sake, so that you may have a share with Him in heaven.

16.15.s.en: (5) Justice and keeping away from the worship of idols

16.15.0.en: Officers: leaders, agents of authority, local heads.

16.15.1.en: Moses commands them to appoint judges and officers for themselves in all their cities when they settle in the Promised Land, so that they may judge with justice in the disputes and problems among people, and so that they may live in safety and peace.

16.16.0.en: God set for Moses three strict principles for judgment:

16.16.1.en: 1- Thou shalt not wrest judgment: that is, do not deviate in your judgment in favor of one party at the expense of the other.

16.16.2.en: 2- Thou shalt not respect persons: that is, do not take into account, when judging, the persons of the disputants; everyone is equal before the law, so there is no flattery of the rich or the notable and no pity for the guilty among the poor.

16.16.3.en: 3- Neither take a gift: Moses made clear that the reason for the prohibition of taking a bribe is that it blinds the eyes of the wise, that is, it makes the sensible close their eyes to the truth and so they issue false judgments. Likewise the Book of Numbers showed them that bribery perverts the words of the righteous, for it is tempting and affects judges even if they are honorable, and makes them utter words contrary to what they know in their hearts to be the truth.

16.17.0.en: The repetition of the word justice here is to stress the necessity of following the truth and keeping away from injustice in judgments. And he promised them that if they follow justice in their judgments they will live, that is, their existence as a nation will continue and they will live a safe, settled life and ensure that they deserve to remain in the land the Lord gave them, so that He does not drive them out of it as a recompense for disobedience and injustice.

16.18.0.en: The grove: a pillar set up on high places (it may be of wood or other material) or a tree planted beside the pagan altar.

16.18.1.en: The Lord forbids the manifestations of pagan worship that existed in the region, so that His people may not imitate what the other peoples do; the Lord commands them not to set up pillars or plant trees beside the altar they build for the Lord.

16.19.0.en: The image: a pillar of stones.

16.19.1.en: Likewise they are not to set up stone pillars for the same purpose, so that they do not imitate the pagans in their worship and superstitions and do not practice their rites and so fall into the same errors, because the Lord hates such works and practices and is angry with those who practice them.

16.19.2.en: Do not rush to judge anyone, lest you err unintentionally. And before you pass a judgment, seek God to receive His guidance and to feel that you are in His presence, so that you will be just in your judgments.

16.19.3.en: The counsel of the priest, laws for the king, and the worship of idols
